1: Some people set aside the rule of scripture and yet sacrifice full of faith. Where do they stand, Kṛṣṇa? Is it in sattva, in rajas or in tamas?
2: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, and it is born of their own nature: it is of sattva, of rajas or of tamas. Hear about it now.
3: Everyone's faith is in keeping with their nature, descendant of Bharata. A person is made of faith. Whatever one's faith is, that is what one is.
4: Those of sattva worship the gods, and those of rajas worship the yakṣas and rākṣasas. The others, the people of tamas, worship the departed and the hosts of spirits.
5: There are people who practise fierce austerities that scripture does not ordain. They are bound up in hypocrisy and ego, and driven by the force of desire and passion.
6: Senseless, they torment the group of elements that dwells in the body, and they torment me as well, dwelling within the body. Know them to be demonic in their resolve.
7: The food that each person loves is also of three kinds, and so are sacrifice, austerity and giving. Hear how they differ.
8: Foods that increase life, vitality, strength, health, happiness and delight, that are juicy, oily, firm and pleasing to the heart, are dear to a person of sattva.
9: Foods that are pungent, sour, salty, very hot, sharp, dry and burning are what a person of rajas wants. They bring pain, grief and sickness.
10: Food that is stale, that has lost its taste, that is putrid and has been left overnight, that is also other people's leavings and unfit to be offered, is dear to a person of tamas.
11: A sacrifice is of sattva when it is the one the rule lays down, and is offered by those who do not long for its fruit, with the mind settled on the thought that it simply ought to be offered.
12: But when a sacrifice is offered with its fruit in view, and for the sake of show as well, best of the Bharatas, know that sacrifice to be of rajas.
13: A sacrifice that ignores the rule, where no food is given out, no sacred words are spoken and no gift is made to the priest, and that is empty of faith, is declared to be of tamas.
14: Honouring the gods, the twice-born, the teachers and the wise, together with purity, uprightness, celibacy and doing no harm: this is called austerity of the body.
15: Speech that upsets no one, that is true, pleasant and helpful, and also the regular practice of one's own recitation: this is called austerity of speech.
16: Calmness of mind, gentleness, silence, restraint of the self and purity of feeling: this is called austerity of the mind.
17: When this threefold austerity is practised with the highest faith, by disciplined people who do not long for its fruit, it is declared to be of sattva.
18: Austerity that is done to win good treatment, respect and honour, and done with hypocrisy too, is said here to be of rajas. It is unsteady and does not last.
19: Austerity that is done out of a deluded notion, with torment of the self, or in order to destroy someone else, is declared to be of tamas.
20: A gift is remembered as being of sattva when it is given simply because it ought to be given, to someone who does no favour in return, in the right place, at the right time and to a worthy receiver.
21: But a gift that is given to get a favour in return, or else with some fruit in view, and that is given grudgingly, is remembered as being of rajas.
22: A gift that is given in the wrong place and at the wrong time, to unworthy receivers, without courtesy and with contempt, is declared to be of tamas.
23: Oṁ, tat, sat: this is remembered as the threefold designation of brahman. By it the brahmins, the Vedas and the sacrifices were ordained long ago.
24: So those who speak of brahman always utter oṁ before they begin the acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity that the rules lay down.
25: With the word tat, and with no fruit in view, those who long for release perform acts of sacrifice and austerity and the various acts of giving.
26: The word sat is used to mean what is real and to mean what is good. In the same way, son of Pṛthā, the word sat is applied to an action worthy of praise.
27: Steadiness in sacrifice, in austerity and in giving is also called sat. And action done for the sake of that is simply named sat as well.
28: Whatever is offered in the fire, given, practised as austerity or done without faith is called asat, son of Pṛthā. It is nothing after one departs, and nothing here.
